name: Galápagos Islands

pin.note: Approximate centre of the archipelago (0°30′S 90°30′W), as given in the Wikipedia article infobox; it is not any single island. UNESCO's own coordinate string is malformed so was not used.

creatures.iucn_status: Extinct (IUCN Red List; assessment Cayot et al., 2016 per two secondary sources; Wikipedia says the assessment was amended in 2022)
creatures.status_note: The last known pure individual, Lonesome George, died 24 June 2012. Hybrids with Pinta ancestry were found on Volcano Wolf, Isabela, so purebred relatives may survive. The IUCN Red List site could not be fetched directly.
creatures.home_note: Pinta Island coordinates (0°35′14″N 90°45′44″W) from the Wikipedia article infobox.

creatures.status_note: GBIF match returned ACCEPTED species, EXACT match, confidence 99, usageKey 2433460 (Zalophus wollebaeki Sivertsen, 1953). IUCN site blocked WebFetch (robots), so Endangered is verified from two secondary sources (Wikipedia, citing a 2015 assessment; Animal Diversity Web). Not confirmed on iucnredlist.org.

facts.statement: The archipelago lies in the Pacific Ocean roughly 1,000 km from mainland Ecuador.
facts.source_title: Galápagos Islands - UNESCO World Heritage Centre
facts.evidence_note: Location line of the property description.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Wikipedia gives the group's coordinates as 0°30′S 90°30′W, i.e. just south of the equator in the eastern Pacific.
facts.evidence_note: Infobox coordinates.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The group comprises 127 islands, islets and rocks, of which 19 are large and 4 are inhabited.
facts.source_title: Galápagos Islands - UNESCO World Heritage Centre
facts.evidence_note: Description of the property's islands.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Wolf volcano, the archipelago's highest, sits at the north end of Isabela and straddles the equator, at about 0.02°N, 91.35°W.
facts.evidence_note: Coordinates and location text on the volcano page.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The cooler garúa season runs June to November, with sea and air near 22 °C, steady wind, drizzle and heavy fog or mist.
facts.evidence_note: Climate section season description.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The warm season, December to May, has average sea and air temperatures of about 25 °C, little wind, and sunshine broken by occasional heavy downpours.
facts.evidence_note: Climate section season description.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: San Cristóbal's 1981-2010 normals show an annual mean temperature of 24.8 °C and annual precipitation of about 578 mm over 119 days.
facts.evidence_note: Climate table/normals for San Cristóbal.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Rainfall on Santa Cruz in 1969 ranged from 469.7 mm at the Charles Darwin Station on the coast to 2,656.4 mm at the highland Media Luna site.
facts.evidence_note: Santa Cruz rainfall paragraph.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Five major ocean currents converge on the islands, including the cold Humboldt Current and the eastward Cromwell Current, which wells up nutrient-rich water.
facts.evidence_note: Ocean currents article text.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The highest point in the archipelago is Volcán Wolf on Isabela, at 1,707 m.
facts.evidence_note: Geography section / infobox.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Smithsonian lists Wolf as a shield volcano of 1,710 m whose most recent eruption ran from 6 January to 14 April 2022.
facts.evidence_note: Elevation and eruptive history fields.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Isabela formed from six merged shield volcanoes: Alcedo, Cerro Azul, Darwin, Ecuador, Sierra Negra and Wolf.
facts.evidence_note: Geology paragraph.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The islands sit over a mantle plume (hotspot) beneath the Nazca Plate, which drifts east-southeast at about 6.4 cm per year.
facts.evidence_note: Geology section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Island ages increase to the east, from Fernandina at about 0.05 million years to San Cristóbal at about 3.2 million years.
facts.evidence_note: Geology table of island ages.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Bishop Tomás de Berlanga, whose ship drifted off course, reached the islands on 10 March 1535.
facts.evidence_note: History section on discovery.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Charles Darwin arrived aboard HMS Beagle on 15 September 1835.
facts.evidence_note: History section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Ecuador annexed the archipelago on 12 February 1832 in a ceremony on Floreana.
facts.evidence_note: History section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Galápagos National Park was established on 4 July 1959.
facts.evidence_note: Establishment details in lead.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The islands were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1978, the Marine Reserve was created in 1986 and extended in 1998.
facts.source_title: Galápagos Islands - UNESCO World Heritage Centre
facts.evidence_note: Inscription and extension history.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: UNESCO's World Heritage Committee put the Galápagos on its 'in danger' list on 26 June 2007 citing invasive species, tourism and immigration.
facts.evidence_note: Article text on the Christchurch committee decision.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The islands form Ecuador's Galápagos Province, with Puerto Baquerizo Moreno as capital and three cantons: Isabela, San Cristóbal and Santa Cruz.
facts.evidence_note: Infobox and lead.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The 2022 census counted 28,583 residents, 22,741 of them urban.
facts.evidence_note: Population line.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Ecuador's constitution sets a special regime (régimen especial) for the islands, and draft legislation defined four migration categories, with only permanent residents free of time limits.
facts.source_title: Proyecto de Ley de Galápagos responde a construcción participativa
facts.evidence_note: Press summary of the draft special law.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The property holds about 500 vascular plant species (about 180 endemic) and 36 reptile species, all endemic.
facts.source_title: Galápagos Islands - UNESCO World Heritage Centre
facts.evidence_note: Ecology paragraph.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Around 2,909 marine species are recorded, with 18.2% endemism.
facts.source_title: Galápagos Islands - UNESCO World Heritage Centre
facts.evidence_note: Ecology paragraph.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: About 43% of land plants, 56% of insects and roughly 80% of land birds are found only on the islands.
facts.evidence_note: Endemism passage.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Galápagos Marine Reserve covers 133,000 km2, and the site's convergence of three currents drives rich marine ecosystems.
facts.source_title: Galápagos Islands - UNESCO World Heritage Centre
facts.evidence_note: Property area and description.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Over 500 non-native plant species have been recorded, and rats, feral goats and cats and introduced insects harm native wildlife.
facts.evidence_note: Invasive species passage.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Reporting on the 2007 listing says goats compete with tortoises for food and up to 80,000 were removed over three years.
facts.evidence_note: Article body.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Roughly 97% of the land and 99% of marine areas are protected, and a USD 20 million invasive species fund (FEIG) was set up in 2011.
facts.evidence_note: Protected area and funding passages.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: UNESCO lists the site as removed from the danger list in 2010 after being on it from 2007.
facts.source_title: Galápagos Islands - UNESCO World Heritage Centre
facts.evidence_note: Danger listing history.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Chelonoidis abingdonii, the Pinta Island tortoise, is listed as Extinct on the IUCN Red List (assessment Cayot et al., 2016, as cited).
facts.evidence_note: Status line citing the IUCN assessment.
facts.subject: pinta-island-tortoise

facts.statement: Lonesome George was found dead on 24 June 2012 by his caretaker Fausto Llerena after about 40 years of care.
facts.evidence_note: Death section.
facts.subject: pinta-island-tortoise

facts.statement: Wikipedia reports that goats introduced to Pinta in 1958 stripped vegetation and Pinta was declared goat-free in 2003.
facts.evidence_note: Threats section.
facts.subject: pinta-island-tortoise

facts.statement: Pinta Island is about 60 km2 and reaches 650 m; whalers took an estimated 455 tortoises there between 1831 and 1868.
facts.publisher: Reptiles of Ecuador (Pontificia Universidad Católica del Ecuador)
facts.evidence_note: Distribution and threats.
facts.subject: pinta-island-tortoise

facts.statement: A 2013 study found 17 tortoises with Pinta ancestry among over 1,600 sampled on Volcano Wolf, Isabela.
facts.source_title: The genetic legacy of Lonesome George survives (Edwards et al. 2013, Biological Conservation)
facts.evidence_note: Abstract summary.
facts.subject: pinta-island-tortoise

facts.statement: A 2012 Yale expedition found 17 first-generation-type hybrids at Wolf Volcano, and in 2020 a young female with direct Pinta ancestry was reported.
facts.evidence_note: Hybrids section.
facts.subject: pinta-island-tortoise

facts.statement: GBIF's backbone matches Chelonoidis abingdonii (Günther, 1877) as an accepted species in family Testudinidae (usageKey 7451150).
facts.source_title: GBIF Backbone Taxonomy species match: Chelonoidis abingdonii
facts.evidence_note: Match result.
facts.subject: pinta-island-tortoise

facts.statement: The Galápagos sea lion is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List, and the assessment cited for this listing dates from 2015.
facts.evidence_note: Conservation status section cites a 2015 IUCN assessment with Endangered category.
facts.subject: galapagos-sea-lion

facts.statement: Population estimates for the Galápagos sea lion fluctuate between roughly 20,000 and 50,000 animals; the source gives no year for this range.
facts.evidence_note: Population section gives the 20,000-50,000 range without a date.
facts.subject: galapagos-sea-lion

facts.statement: A 2024 census cruise reported 3,601 Galápagos sea lions counted across breeding sites, alongside 2,162 Galápagos fur seals.
facts.source_title: Más de 23.000 iguanas y 5.800 lobos marinos viven en Galápagos, revela censo de especies
facts.evidence_note: Census results article breaks down the roughly 5,800 pinnipeds counted by species; this is a count at breeding sites, not a total population estimate.
facts.subject: galapagos-sea-lion

facts.statement: Galápagos sea lions live and breed on all the main Galápagos islands and several smaller ones, have colonised Isla de la Plata, and have been sighted from mainland Ecuador north to Isla Gorgona, Colombia.
facts.evidence_note: Distribution section lists main islands, Isla de la Plata and sightings to Gorgona.
facts.subject: galapagos-sea-lion

facts.statement: Galápagos sea lions feed mainly on sardines plus crustaceans, squid, lanternfish and octopus, and foraging trips can reach 10-15 km from shore and last several days.
facts.evidence_note: Diet and foraging section gives prey list and trip distance.
facts.subject: galapagos-sea-lion

facts.statement: Breeding runs from May to January, a female bears a single pup after about 11 months of gestation, and pups are weaned at roughly 11 months, though some mothers nurse a pup for up to three years.
facts.evidence_note: Reproduction section describes season, single pup, weaning age and extended nursing.
facts.subject: galapagos-sea-lion

facts.statement: El Niño warming reduces the sea lions' food supply and can cause population declines and die-offs; the early-1980s El Niño killed many yearlings and lowered pup production the next year.
facts.source_title: Zalophus wollebaeki (Galapagos sea lion) - Animal Diversity Web
facts.publisher: Animal Diversity Web (University of Michigan Museum of Zoology)
facts.evidence_note: Conservation and threats discussion links the 1980s El Niño to yearling deaths and reduced pup production.
facts.subject: galapagos-sea-lion

facts.statement: Feral dogs have been reported to kill young Galápagos sea lions and may transmit canine diseases to the population, according to the Handbook of the Mammals of the World.
facts.source_title: Zalophus wollebaeki Sivertsen 1953 (Handbook of the Mammals of the World, Vol. 4)
facts.publisher: Lynx Edicions (Mittermeier and Wilson), via Zenodo/Plazi
facts.evidence_note: Threats section covers stray dog packs, disease and fishing entanglement; Animal Diversity Web also names feral dogs as a threat. Re-checked 2026-10-09 against Lynx Edicions (Mittermeier and Wilson), via Zenodo/Plazi; the statement keeps only the parts that source supports. Dogs/disease confirmed by this handbook chapter and Animal Diversity Web; fishing-net entanglement not confirmed there (only a pinnipeds.org page of ~2000 data mentions it), so that half is left out.
facts.subject: galapagos-sea-lion

facts.statement: An annual monitoring cruise run by the Galápagos National Park Directorate with Universidad San Francisco de Quito and the biosecurity agency surveys sea lions and fur seals at 30 breeding sites on 14 islands and samples animals to assess health.
facts.source_title: Galápagos sea lion and fur seal monitoring cruise
facts.evidence_note: Article describes the cruise partners, site count and health sampling funded through Galápagos Conservancy grants. 2026-10-09: the source link now returns HTTP 404 and no replacement page confirming the monitoring cruise details (30 sites, 14 islands) was found. Treat as unverified.
facts.subject: galapagos-sea-lion

facts.statement: A mother sea lion can pick out her own pup's bark from among 30 or more barking sea lions, and territorial males bark more often than non-territorial males.
facts.evidence_note: Behaviour section describes pup-bark recognition and male barking frequency.
facts.subject: galapagos-sea-lion

facts.statement: The Galápagos penguin (Spheniscus mendiculus) is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List according to Wikipedia, which cites the 2020 assessment; about 90% of the birds live on Fernandina and the west coast of Isabela, and the page gives about 1,200 mature birds as of 2018.
facts.evidence_note: Conservation status and population sections. The page's population figures (1,200 in 2018, 1,351 in 2003, about 1,800 elsewhere) come from different dates and are inconsistent; the status was not checked on iucnredlist.org. Scientific name verified against the GBIF backbone API (api.gbif.org/v1/species/match, EXACT match); the name was not read on the Wikipedia page itself.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Wikipedia reports that El Niño cut the Galápagos penguin population by 77% in 1982-83 and by 65% in 1997-98, because warmer water reduces the upwelling and plankton the birds' prey depends on.
facts.evidence_note: El Niño effects section; figures are as reported by the page, underlying studies not checked.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The flightless cormorant (Phalacrocorax harrisi) is listed as Vulnerable (IUCN 3.1) per Wikipedia, which gives 1,679 individuals in a 2011 estimate and a range limited to Fernandina and the northern and western coasts of Isabela.
facts.evidence_note: Status, population and range sections. Page says it was downlisted from Endangered in 2011. Name Phalacrocorax harrisi is the GBIF accepted name (Nannopterum harrisi is a GBIF synonym); verified via GBIF species API, not the Wikipedia page.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The waved albatross (Phoebastria irrorata) is classed as Critically Endangered (IUCN 3.1) per Wikipedia, which gives about 34,700 adult birds from a 2001 estimate and says it breeds primarily on Española Island, with longline fishing singled out as having a severe impact on the species.
facts.evidence_note: Status, population, breeding and threats sections. Scientific name verified against the GBIF backbone API (api.gbif.org/v1/species/match, EXACT match); the name was not read on the Wikipedia page itself. Statement corrected after an independent re-read of the source.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Galápagos fur seal (Arctocephalus galapagoensis) is described by Wikipedia as classified as an endangered species, is endemic to the archipelago and present on nearly all its islands, with most seals found in the northern and western areas, and lost about 30% of its adults and almost all pups in the 1982-83 El Niño.
facts.evidence_note: Status, habitat and El Niño sections. The page gives the population estimate as about 30,000 but dates it inconsistently (1970 and late 1970s). Scientific name verified against the GBIF backbone API (api.gbif.org/v1/species/match, EXACT match); the name was not read on the Wikipedia page itself. Statement corrected after an independent re-read of the source.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The marine iguana (Amblyrhynchus cristatus) is listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN according to Wikipedia, which puts the archipelago-wide total at roughly 200,000 to 300,000 with considerable uncertainty and says El Niño can cut populations by as much as 90% on some islands.
facts.evidence_note: Status, population and El Niño sections. Scientific name verified against the GBIF backbone API (api.gbif.org/v1/species/match, EXACT match); the name was not read on the Wikipedia page itself.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Galápagos petrel (Pterodroma phaeopygia) is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List per Wikipedia, which estimates 6,000 to 15,000 mature individuals, still declining, nesting mainly in the highlands of five islands including Santiago, Floreana, Isabela, Santa Cruz and San Cristóbal.
facts.evidence_note: Status, population and nesting sections. The page's nest-elevation figure appears to contain a unit error and was not used. Scientific name verified against the GBIF backbone API (api.gbif.org/v1/species/match, EXACT match); the name was not read on the Wikipedia page itself.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The mangrove finch (Camarhynchus heliobates) is listed as Critically Endangered per Wikipedia (BirdLife International assessment 2021), with an estimated 20-40 mature individuals surviving in two mangrove areas on Isabela and no recent records on Fernandina.
facts.evidence_note: Status, population and range sections.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Floreana mockingbird (Mimus trifasciatus) is listed as Endangered (IUCN 3.1) per Wikipedia, was extirpated from Floreana by 1888, and now survives on the islets of Campeón and Gardner-near-Floreana, where more than 250 individuals are believed to live.
facts.evidence_note: Status, islands and history sections; page says the IUCN moved it from Endangered (1994) to Critically Endangered (2008) and back to Endangered (2017). Scientific name verified against the GBIF backbone API (api.gbif.org/v1/species/match, EXACT match); the name was not read on the Wikipedia page itself.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The whale shark (Rhincodon typus) is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List per Wikipedia, and a 2011-2013 study found that 91.5% of whale sharks observed around Darwin Island in the Galápagos were adult females.
facts.evidence_note: Conservation status paragraph and the Galápagos / Darwin Island passage. Global status, not specific to Galápagos. Scientific name verified against the GBIF backbone API (api.gbif.org/v1/species/match, EXACT match); the name was not read on the Wikipedia page itself.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Reef surveys cited by the Charles Darwin Foundation say Galápagos coral reefs suffered an average mortality of 97% in the 1982-83 El Niño, and Wellington Reef off Darwin Island was the only one of 17 original structural reefs to survive.
facts.evidence_note: Section on the 1982-83 El Niño and Wellington Reef.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: An Aqualink buoy installed at Wellington Reef (Darwin Island) on 10 March 2022 recorded a maximum surface temperature of 29.5 °C, a +3.6 °C anomaly, and triggered a NOAA Coral Heat Stress Alert Level 1, where significant bleaching is likely.
facts.evidence_note: 2022 temperature monitoring section; seafloor maximum was reported as 29.1 °C.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A December 2017 survey reported by One Earth found only about 1 to 3 percent coral cover at Santa Cruz and San Cristóbal, while Darwin and Wolf Islands had places with more than 80 percent live coral cover.
facts.source_title: Finding a refuge for corals amid decimated reefs in the Galápagos
facts.evidence_note: Coral cover paragraphs; a news article summarising a research survey, not the paper itself. The article lists bleaching in 1982-83, 1997-98 and a milder 2015 event.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Research summarised by the Galápagos Conservation Trust found macroplastic on 13 of 14 sandy beaches studied on San Cristóbal (east-facing beaches highest), and only about 2% of the macroplastic was identified as coming from the islands, suggesting most arrives on ocean currents.
facts.source_title: Plastic found in Galapagos seawater, beaches and animals
facts.evidence_note: Summary of the San Cristóbal plastics study; a charity summary, original paper not read.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Where the Cromwell Current meets seamounts near the Galápagos in non-El Niño years it is forced upward, bringing nutrient-rich water to the surface, but this upwelling is irregular and does not occur in El Niño years, when waters around the islands become considerably warmer.
facts.evidence_note: Passage on the Galápagos; the page gives inconsistent current depth and length figures, which were not used.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Lack of fresh water limited early visits to the Galápagos, and Wikipedia says two men and ten horses died of thirst there in 1535; Laguna El Junco on San Cristóbal is described as the archipelago's largest freshwater lake.
facts.evidence_note: Freshwater passages of the climate section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A TU Delft study of Santa Cruz island's water supply found that under business as usual only a small portion of future demand to 2044 could be met, and desalination was presented as the most viable way to close the gap.
facts.source_title: Mitigation options for future water scarcity: a case study in Santa Cruz Island (Galapagos Archipelago)
facts.evidence_note: Abstract only; it names rainwater harvesting, greywater recycling, demand management and desalination, and gives no volumes.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Wikipedia says El Niño occurs every 3 to 7 years in the Galápagos, bringing warmer sea surface temperatures, sea-level rise, stronger waves and nutrient depletion in the water.
facts.evidence_note: Climate section. A WWF/CI report gives 2 to 8 years instead; the sources differ on frequency.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Rainfall at the Charles Darwin Station on Santa Cruz was 249.0 mm in March 1969 but only 1.2 mm in March 1970, an example of how strongly El Niño variation drives year-to-year precipitation.
facts.evidence_note: Climate section; the page links the swing to El Niño.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A WWF and Conservation International report says sea level at the Galápagos could rise about one metre by the end of the century, with volcanic uplift on some islands possibly offsetting it and subsidence on others amplifying it.
facts.source_title: Adapting to Climate Change in the Galápagos Islands
facts.evidence_note: Sea level section (2011 report); projection, not an observation.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The 2011 WWF report states the 1982-83 and 1997-98 El Niño events were the most intense on record for the Galápagos, and that El Niño conditions occur every 2 to 8 years.
facts.source_title: Adapting to Climate Change in the Galápagos Islands
facts.evidence_note: El Niño section; differs from Wikipedia's 3 to 7 years.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: AVISO satellite altimetry pages say sea surface temperatures near the Galápagos rose more than 5 °C above normal during the 1997-98 El Niño, whose sea-level anomaly peaked at more than 20 cm.
facts.evidence_note: The 20 cm figure refers to the Pacific-wide anomaly, and the page does not date the Galápagos warming precisely.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Wikipedia describes Darwin's finches as a group of about 18 species, of which all but the Cocos finch are found only in the Galápagos.
facts.evidence_note: Taxonomy and range sections; the fetched summary is inconsistent on the exact phrasing of endemism. Statement corrected after an independent re-read of the source.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The parasitic fly Philornis downsi was first recorded in Darwin's finch nests on Santa Cruz in 1997, though present in the Galápagos since at least the 1960s, and is a major cause of nestling mortality that threatens rarer species such as the mangrove finch.
facts.evidence_note: Detection and effect sections.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Wikipedia says the giant tortoise population fell from about 250,000 when first discovered in the 16th century to a low of roughly 15,000 in the 1970s, and was about 19,317 in a 1995-2009 estimate.
facts.evidence_note: Population section; the page also gives 3,060 from a 1974 census as an alternative low, so the sources differ. Re-check note: Page intro says ~250,000 and ~15,000 in 1970s; 19,317 matches (a later section gives 3,060 in a 1974 census, so a conflicting figure exists on the page).
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Project Isabela, which ran 1997 to 2006 (action begun in 1999), removed goats from northern Isabela, Santiago and Pinta; Wikipedia gives about 150,000 goats eradicated, though a cited article title says 250,000.
facts.evidence_note: Numbers and dates paragraph; the goat total conflicts between the page text and a cited title. Statement corrected after an independent re-read of the source.
facts.subject: island

gaps: IUCN Red List page itself was blocked by robots/403; status taken from secondary sites and Wikipedia
Official Galápagos National Park Directorate and NOAA/NASA pages not retrieved
Current visitor numbers (sources disagree) not included
Lonesome George age and carapace measurements not firmly sourced
[sea lion] IUCN Red List page not fetchable (robots disallowed); category and 2015 year are secondary-sourced.
[sea lion] No peer-reviewed paper could be fetched (PMC returned reCAPTCHA; Europe PMC rate limited); NOAA fetch not approved; Darwin Foundation datazone had no record.
[sea lion] Population estimate (20,000-50,000) has no stated year in the source.
conflicts: Land area: Wikipedia gives 8,010 km2 in the infobox but 7,880 km2 in the body; province page gives 7,882 km2 land.
Garúa season: Wikipedia says June-November; MIT course page says July-December. Facts use the Wikipedia dates.
Population: Wikipedia gives 33,042 (2020) and 28,583 (2022 census); UNESCO says about 30,000.
Lonesome George's discovery: Wikipedia says 1 Dec 1971, another Wikipedia page says 1 Nov 1971, Galápagos Conservancy says 1971, a species database cites 1974. Not used as a fact.
Goats on Pinta: introduced 1958 (Wikipedia) vs 1959 (Galápagos Conservancy).
IUCN assessment year: 2016 (Cayot et al., via secondary sites) vs 'amended 2022' (Wikipedia).
World Heritage inscription: UNESCO says 1978; Wikipedia national park page says 1979.
Al Jazeera cited 'invertebrate' figures internally inconsistent (53 vs 55); not used.

[sea lion] GAL-102 (20,000-50,000 population estimate, undated) versus GAL-103 (3,601 counted at breeding sites in 2024) are different measures, not a true contradiction; do not present 3,601 as total population.
